one_liner: Google's synchronous C++ stream logger (LOG, CHECK, VLOG); about 4x faster than Boost.Log 1.56 file logging in 2014 tests.
what_it_does: glog provides LOG(severity) << ... stream macros, CHECK/DCHECK assertions, VLOG with per-module verbosity (--vmodule), per-severity log files, a failure signal handler that prints a stack trace, and pluggable LogSink objects. Behaviour is controlled by global FLAGS_* variables, gflags command-line flags or GLOG_* environment variables. It is not a drop-in for Boost.Log: there are no attribute sets, filters or sink frontends, just macros and global flags.
how_it_is_fast: Each message is formatted into a preallocated per-thread buffer (thread_local LogMessageData holding a fixed 30,000-byte array), then written under one global std::mutex with fwrite to a stdio FILE*. INFO lines are buffered by default (logbuflevel=0) and flushed only every 1,000,000 bytes or every logbufsecs=30 seconds, and on Linux written log pages are dropped from the page cache with posix_fadvise. The Boost.Log side of the benchmark did more work per record: it added common attributes (line id, timestamp, process and thread id), ran a severity filter and a timestamp formatter.
when_to_use: Existing glog code bases, or code that relies on CHECK/DCHECK, VLOG with --vmodule and InstallFailureSignalHandler stack traces as one package.
Moderate-rate application logging to local files where a synchronous call of a microsecond or so is acceptable and Boost.Log's setup and per-record cost are not.
Low-level code that needs a lock-free, allocation-free path: RAW_LOG in <glog/raw_logging.h>.
Migration work: keep the glog API and move to ng-log, which describes itself as API-compatible.
when_not_to_use: New projects: the repository was archived on 2025-06-30; its README points to ng-log or Abseil Logging.
Latency-critical hot paths: every LOG call formats and writes synchronously under a global mutex, while async loggers in this category report single-digit to low hundreds of nanoseconds per call.
Many threads logging heavily: in the spdlog runs, 10 threads were slower than 1 (1.68-3.55 s vs about 1.1 s wall) and the 10-thread run spent 6.2 s of system time.
Crash-sensitive audit logs: buffered INFO lines (up to 30 s or 1 MB) are lost on a hard crash unless FLAGS_logbuflevel is set to -1, which flushes every line and gives up most of the measured speed.
Format-string or structured logging: the API is ostream-only, and messages longer than 30,000 bytes are truncated.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake or Bazel)
integration.dependencies: Threads; optional gflags 2.2.2, libunwind or unwind for stack traces, dbghelp on Windows; GTest only for tests
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (CMake target_compile_features cxx_std_14 at HEAD; the measured 0.3.3 release predates that)
integration.platforms: Linux and other Unix-likes, macOS, Windows and Cygwin (platform branches in CMakeLists.txt); stack traces need libunwind, unwind or dbghelp
integration.thread_safety: LOG/CHECK are thread-safe and serialised by a global std::mutex; AddLogSink/RemoveLogSink are thread-safe; LogSink::send must not call LOG or CHECK (deadlock); EnableLogCleaner thread safety is questioned in open issue #753

gotchas: Benchmark harness flaw (spdlog bench at dc198a5): the two sides were not set up alike. glog wrote its full prefix (date, microseconds, thread id, file:line) and used default buffering. Boost.Log wrote '[timestamp]: message' through a filter, a formatter and a 10 MiB rotating sink with auto_flush=false. Wall time came from `time ./binary`, so process start-up is included, and Boost 1.56 was linked dynamically from a personal build with unstated flags.
Default INFO buffering (logbuflevel=0, logbufsecs=30, flush every 1,000,000 bytes) is part of why the numbers look good; the tail of the log is lost on SIGKILL or power loss.
Flags are process-global: FLAGS_log_dir must be set before InitGoogleLogging, and if the log file cannot be created glog prints 'COULD NOT CREATE LOGFILE' to stderr.
Messages logged before InitGoogleLogging() go to stderr with a one-time warning.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick glog (or its successor ng-log) for the CHECK/VLOG/failure-handler bundle or an existing code base, not for speed: loguru's own benchmark has it about 1.8x faster than glog 0.6.0, BqLog and Coost report glog far behind, and Quill, NanoLog or fmtlog cut call-site latency to nanoseconds. Over Boost.Log, glog is the simpler and, in these old tests, about 4x faster synchronous file logger.
verified_claims_summary: In spdlog's 2014 benchmark (Ubuntu 64-bit, Intel i7-4770, bench programs built with g++ -O3 -flto -march=native, system libglog 0.3.3, Boost.Log 1.56), writing 1M lines to files took glog 1.077 s vs Boost.Log 4.207 s on one thread and 1.678 vs 6.592 s on 10 threads (3.9x). Later runs on the same machine gave 1.115 vs 4.430 s and 2.027 vs 13.985 s (bench/results.txt at def6fc6) and best-of-3 1.109 vs 4.779 s and 3.546 vs 15.151 s, so 4.0-4.3x on one thread and 3.9-6.9x on 10 threads (ratios derived from page data); spdlog's synchronous logger beat glog on one thread in every run.
status_note: Abandoned: archived read-only on 2025-06-30 (last release 0.7.1, June 2024; HEAD CMake says 0.8.0). It is still BSD-3-Clause, widely packaged and copyable, but new work should go to ng-log (community, API-compatible) or Abseil Logging.
